messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 62

He is a 60-year-old European man who comes across as sturdy and practical, the kind of person who has spent most of his life working with his hands and keeping to routines. He has lived with his partner for several years now, and he speaks about her with clear affection, though he also admits that she has learned to read the signs when he begins to pull away. He works in a warehouse, where the noise, the repetition, and the physical demands suit him better than jobs that require too much sitting still or too much talking. He says he has always liked being useful, liked jobs where the day makes sense.

His difficulties begin in the military, during a deployment that still feels to him less like a memory than an event that is waiting somewhere in the room with him. He describes one night in particular, when a sudden attack changes everything. He had been on edge for days before that, sleeping lightly, listening for changes in the dark, but when the shelling starts he is thrown into a kind of helplessness he had never known. He remembers the sound more than anything else at first: the sharp crack, the screaming metal, the frantic shouting of other men trying to make sense of what is happening. He remembers dirt in his mouth, the weight of his body pressed to the ground, and the moment he realizes that the man beside him is not getting up. He does not talk about that night as if it belongs fully in the past; he talks about it as though he is still there, still hearing it, still trying to understand why he lived and others did not.

After the deployment, he returns home with the expectation that relief will come if he can just get back to ordinary life. Instead, ordinary life feels strange and thin. He notices he cannot sit with his back to a door. He scans parking lots without meaning to. He becomes impatient in crowded stores and avoids places where people stand too close behind him. Loud bangs make his whole body jerk before his mind can tell him what the sound is. Fireworks are unbearable. Even the backfire of a car can send him into a sweat, his heart racing so hard that he has to grip the edge of a counter until the feeling passes.

At night, the memories come in pieces. Sometimes he dreams he is back in the field, unable to move, listening for the next blast. Other times he wakes without any dream at all, already frightened, his body braced as if something is about to happen. He describes lying awake in bed with his partner beside him, careful not to wake her, watching the ceiling and waiting for dawn. He is tired in a way that sleep does not fix. He gets through the day by keeping busy and avoiding anything that might let his mind drift. If he stops moving, the images come. He tells himself not to think about it, and for a while that works, but the effort leaves him tense and exhausted.

Over the years, he becomes a man who keeps emotions under tight control. He says he has always believed that talking about what happened will not change it, but it is also clear that speaking about the war brings a wave of shame and grief he does not know how to manage. He misses the men who died, and he misses the version of himself who felt competent and calm. He notices that he has become more irritable, quicker to snap at small problems, and then he feels bad afterward, especially when his partner looks hurt and says he is far away even when he is sitting right beside her. He withdraws instead of explaining, and the distance grows.

At work, he functions well enough because the warehouse gives him structure. He likes lifting, sorting, and keeping to the rhythm of the shift. But even there, certain sounds can catch him off guard, and he has to pause to steady himself. He prefers tasks done alone or with a few trusted coworkers. He does not speak much about himself. He has learned to hide how much effort it takes just to stay settled in his own skin.

In recent sessions, he describes feeling as though the war still reaches into the present, appearing in flashes and then disappearing before he can catch hold of it. He is increasingly aware that his body reacts before his thoughts do, that fear lives in him as much as memory does. He wants to remain dependable, useful, and close to the woman he loves, but there are moments when he feels split between the life he is living now and the one that was interrupted decades ago, as if part of him is still listening for danger in the dark.
